description:
Garage single-node object storage. Garage ships no admin UI, so this dashboard is the operator console: it is the only place bucket-store health, capacity and reclamation are visible.

A panel reading "No data" here is not necessarily broken. Grafana cannot render custom empty-state text when a query returns no series at all, so a metric that has never been emitted looks identical to a failing panel. Where zero is the truthful reading, the query coalesces to an explicit zero line rather than relying on that text. Where zero would be a false claim -- an undefined ratio, or a series nothing has started emitting yet -- the panel is deliberately left empty instead of asserting a zero. Each panel's description says which of the two it is, and the module README lists what Garage does not expose at all.

panels.description: up{job="garage"} -- whether Prometheus successfully scraped Garage's admin API on its last attempt. This is a single-node deployment: if it is down the S3, website and admin APIs are unavailable, not degraded. Backs the GarageNodeDown alert (fires after 5m).
panels.title: Garage

panels.description: The running Garage build, read from the version label of garage_build_info. The module pins this by digest, so a change here means the pinned image actually rolled -- not that Garage upgraded itself.
panels.title: Version

panels.description:
Rows in Garage's object table (table_size{table_name="object"}) -- the closest thing Garage exposes to "how many S3 objects do I have". One row per key, including delete-marker tombstones not yet collected and in-flight uploads, so it approximates the S3 object count rather than matching it exactly.

Garage publishes no per-bucket or per-key dimension on any metric, so this is every bucket summed and cannot be split by consumer. Splitting Loki's usage from Authentik's requires the admin API (GET /v2/GetBucketInfo), not Prometheus.
panels.title: Objects stored

panels.description:
table_size{table_name="version"} / table_size{table_name="object"}.

Garage implements no S3 object versioning, and its object table drops every version older than the last complete one on merge -- so there is no version history to accumulate and this sits near 1 in a healthy steady state. What it does catch is version rows outliving the objects that referenced them: rows awaiting table GC, multipart uploads, and in-flight writes. A ratio that climbs and stays up means the version table is not being collected, which is the Garage-native shape of the reclamation failure that made MinIO consume 3.2x its live data.
panels.title: Versions per object

panels.description:
Data corruptions Garage has detected on block reads.

block_corruption_counter is a lazily-bound OpenTelemetry instrument: it is absent from a healthy node's /metrics entirely rather than present and zero, so a bare query over it could not tell "no corruptions" apart from "Garage was never deployed". The `or (0 * max(up))` term resolves that into three distinguishable states: absent when Garage is not being scraped at all, an explicit 0 when Garage is up and has recorded none, and a real count when it has.

This is PR #3648's recording-rule logic inlined rather than a reference to object_store:recovery_block_corruptions_total. That was the original intent, but the rule has not shipped, and a panel keyed to a series that does not exist yet is blind in exactly the way this coalescing exists to prevent -- it would read "No data" whether or not the store was corrupting. Inlining costs one line and makes the panel true today; the recorded series can be swapped back in once #3648 lands, with no change in meaning.

Feeds the recovery-events KPI on issue #3611, whose pass bar is zero over 30 days.
panels.title: Block corruptions

panels.description:
1 - garage_local_disk_avail/garage_local_disk_total for the metadata volume, which Garage computes live with statvfs on every scrape.

Metadata is the volume that matters on this workload: 95.4% of objects are under 1 KB and Garage stores objects below 3072 bytes inline in LMDB, so they consume metadata rather than data blocks. Backs the GarageLowDiskSpace alert, which fires below 10% free (90% used).
panels.title: Metadata volume used

panels.description:
Garage alert conditions currently firing or pending, from the PrometheusRule that ships with this module.

This estate deliberately runs AlertManager unwired -- alerts evaluate and are queryable but route to nobody. That makes this table the only place a Garage alert is ever surfaced, which is why it is on the dashboard rather than assumed to be someone else's job.

Empty is the healthy state: ALERTS series exist only while an alert is pending or firing.

Left uncoalesced on purpose, unlike the S3 panels. A zero row would have to be fabricated -- there is no alert to name, no state and no severity to put in it -- and for a table of *active* alerts, Grafana's "No data" and "nothing is firing" are the same statement to a reader. This is the one panel where the default empty state already says the right thing.
panels.title: Firing / pending Garage alerts

panels.description:
Fraction of each Garage volume in use, from garage_local_disk_avail / garage_local_disk_total -- Garage's own statvfs reading, taken fresh on every scrape.

The red line at 90% is where GarageLowDiskSpace fires. With one node and no peer, there is nowhere else for writes to land once a volume fills. Watch the slope as much as the level: at ~3,095 new objects/day the useful question is time-to-full, not today's percentage.
panels.title: Volume utilisation

panels.description:
PROXY, not a direct measurement. Garage exposes no live-bytes series anywhere in its Prometheus surface -- no stored-bytes, no per-bucket usage -- so the consumed/live ratio PR #3648 builds for MinIO cannot be reproduced for Garage. What follows is the closest substitute the metric surface can support.

Bytes occupied on the metadata volume divided by the object-table row count. This is the amplification proxy that matters for this workload: 95.4% of objects are under 1 KB, and Garage stores anything under 3072 bytes inline in LMDB, so the overwhelming majority of live data lives on the metadata volume rather than as data blocks.

Read it as a shape, not a number. Flat means metadata grows in step with the objects in it. A curve that climbs while the object count is flat means the LMDB store is consuming disk without live rows behind it -- uncollected version/tombstone rows, or free pages LMDB never returns -- which is the Garage-native form of the failure that went unseen on MinIO for months (44 GB consumed against 13.58 GB live, 3.2x).

It cannot separate that from objects simply getting larger. If it climbs, confirm against the GC backlog and table row-count panels before concluding anything.

Baseline from H1 at 3.44M objects: 6361.8 MiB of metadata, ~1.94 KiB/object. Blank while the object count is zero.
panels.title: Metadata bytes per object  (PROXY)

panels.description:
PROXY, not a direct measurement. Garage exposes no live-bytes series anywhere in its Prometheus surface -- no stored-bytes, no per-bucket usage -- so a consumed/live amplification ratio cannot be built for Garage at all. That is why the trial's headline KPI is raw bytes consumed per engine (the panel to the right) rather than a ratio. What follows is the closest substitute the metric surface can support for the reclamation question itself.

Bytes occupied on the data volume divided by block_rc_size, the number of blocks Garage's reference-count table says should exist on disk.

The denominator is deliberately blocks, not objects: only objects above 3072 bytes become data blocks at all, so dividing data bytes by the total object count would mostly measure the inline/block mix rather than amplification. Against block_rc_size the reading is direct -- what is on disk over what is supposed to be on disk.

Flat means blocks are being deleted as their references go away. A rising curve means block files are outliving their reference counts: orphaned blocks, the data-volume half of "retention stopped reclaiming". Garage delays block GC by design (BLOCK_GC_DELAY), so a bump after a bulk delete that settles within minutes is expected; a monotonic climb is not.

Blank while no blocks are referenced. Note both series here also include filesystem overhead, which dominates when the store is nearly empty.
panels.title: Data bytes per referenced block  (PROXY)

panels.description:
object_store:disk_used_bytes -- the disk KPI for issue #3611's 30-day trial: raw bytes on disk per engine, taken from kubelet's own statfs read of each engine's PVCs, with no denominator.

It replaces the consumed/live amplification ratio this panel used to draw, which was removed rather than repaired. That ratio divided by minio_cluster_usage_total_bytes and called the result live bytes because that metric excludes delete markers -- but delete markers are zero-byte placeholders, so excluding them subtracts nothing, while the noncurrent versions they stand in front of are counted in full. The denominator was version-inclusive, not live, and already contained most of the accumulation it was supposed to measure. The ratio was also not computable for Garage at all -- Garage publishes no bucket or object byte-total series -- so it could only ever exist for one arm of a two-arm comparison.

Read as a trend across the whole trial, never as a single reading. MinIO's figure is months of accumulated noncurrent versions; Garage's on day one is a fresh copy of the retained window and is trivially smaller for that reason alone, so a post-cutover snapshot flatters Garage for free. The question is whether Garage's curve stays flat while data is written and expired -- MinIO's did not.

Deliberately not coalesced to zero. kubelet emits volume stats only for a PVC that a running pod has mounted, so the garage series is genuinely absent until Garage is running; an explicit 0 would assert that Garage is storing nothing, which is a different and false claim. Both series are summed per namespace, which counts each engine's whole footprint -- MinIO keeps data and metadata on one volume, Garage splits them across two. The minio series retires with the engine (#3644); the garage one is why this panel outlives the trial.
panels.title: Object store disk consumed by engine

panels.description:
table_gc_todo_queue_length, per table. This is the causal signal for whether deletion actually reclaims: entries land on a table's GC queue when rows are superseded or tombstoned, and leave it when Garage collects them.

Healthy is flat at or near zero across every table -- a queue that only ever grows means Garage is accepting deletes while reclaiming nothing, the precise shape of the MinIO defect that motivated this migration, and the one signal here that shows it before the disk does. All twelve tables are plotted deliberately rather than a chosen subset: the point is to catch accumulation somewhere unexpected, and eleven flat zeroes cost one pixel row.

Garage's block GC is delayed by design (BLOCK_GC_DELAY), so a brief non-zero excursion after a bulk delete is normal; a monotonic climb over hours is not.
panels.title: Metadata GC backlog by table

panels.description:
table_size for the four tables that scale with stored data, the count of referenced blocks, and MinIO's object total as a migration comparator. All are counts, so they share an axis.

The shapes to watch, each a distinct way disk gets consumed invisibly:
- version rising faster than object: version rows outliving their objects, i.e. table GC falling behind.
- block_ref rising while object is flat: block references accumulating with no new objects behind them.
- multipart_upload climbing and never falling: abandoned multipart uploads. These hold their blocks indefinitely and are the classic silent consumer of S3 disk -- nothing expires them, and no alert covers it.
- blocks referenced flat while the data volume grows: orphaned block files (see the data-bytes-per-block panel).

The MinIO series is the source side of the bucket migration -- during cutover, the two converging is what "the copy finished" looks like. It vanishes on its own when MinIO is decommissioned, since both engines are deployed by this same module.

Note object counts rows, not live keys: a delete leaves a tombstone row until table GC collects it, and in-flight uploads occupy a row too. It is a good approximation of S3 object count, not an exact one.
panels.title: What is actually stored

panels.description:
rate(api_s3_request_counter) by api_endpoint -- what Garage is actually being asked to do.

The expected shape for this estate is distinctive and worth checking against: ~2.17 ops/sec of which ~86% are LIST, driven by Loki's chunk store. A sudden change in the mix is more informative than a change in total volume -- e.g. GET overtaking LIST would mean something other than Loki has started using this store.

The api_s3_* families are lazily-bound OpenTelemetry instruments: they are absent from /metrics until the first S3 request of that kind is served, and no client has been cut over to Garage yet. The flat zero line is a second query, guarded by `and on() absent(...)`, that exists only while the counter does not -- it disappears by itself the moment real traffic starts, so it can never sit alongside live data. Without it the panel would return no series at all, which Grafana renders as a bare "No data" indistinguishable from a broken query.
panels.title: S3 requests by operation

panels.description:
p99 of api_s3_request_duration, per operation.

The 1s line is the gate H1 pre-registered for this workload (LIST p99 <= 1000 ms at 1.86 LIST/s); Garage measured 271.7 ms against MinIO's 347.9 ms on the same host at 3.44M objects. That benchmark used a closed-loop load generator at n=200 per checkpoint, so treat its p99 as indicative rather than precise -- but this panel measures the real server-side distribution, which the benchmark could not.

targets.legendFormat: no S3 requests served yet (not a latency reading)

panels.title: S3 request latency p99 by operation

panels.description:
rate(api_s3_error_counter) by status_code and operation. Garage only increments this instrument for 4xx and 5xx responses -- 2xx and 3xx never touch it -- so any line here is a real client-visible failure and there is no success traffic to drown it out.

Distinguish the two families before reacting. 5xx is Garage failing. 4xx is usually the client, and on this deployment one 4xx cause is known and specific: Garage validates the SigV4 signing region exactly and rejects a mismatch with AuthorizationHeaderMalformed, where MinIO ignored it entirely. That difference was fatal to Loki's compactor at cutover, not merely degrading, so a burst of 4xx immediately after pointing a new client at Garage is the first thing to check.

The rate of a status code that has never occurred is absent rather than zero -- these are lazily-bound counters, so Garage emits nothing at all until the first failure. The flat zero line is a second query, guarded by `and on() absent(...)`, that exists only while the counter does not; it removes itself the moment a real error is recorded, so it can never sit alongside live data. A zero line here is therefore the healthy state, and is distinguishable from a broken panel -- which is what a bare "No data" would have looked like.
panels.title: S3 errors by status code

panels.description:
block_resync_queue_length (blocks queued for a local consistency check) and block_resync_errored_blocks (block hashes whose last resync attempt failed).

Both are eagerly-registered gauges, so they are present and zero on a healthy node -- unlike most of Garage's counters. On a single node there is no peer to catch up from, so a persistent queue means Garage is not keeping up with its own integrity work rather than that a peer is behind. These back GarageHighBlockResyncQueue (>10000 for 30m) and GarageBlockResyncErrors (>0 for 15m); errored blocks also feed the recovery-events KPI on issue #3611, whose pass bar is zero over 30 days.
panels.title: Block resync queue and errored blocks

panels.description:
Garage routes every table and block operation through its RPC layer, even addressed to itself on a single node, so this reflects internal request health rather than peer connectivity.

Each series is individually wrapped in `or vector(0)` on purpose. All three counters are lazily bound and absent on a healthy node, and in PromQL an empty vector added to anything yields an empty vector -- so a combined expression that sums them without coalescing renders nothing at all, and cannot be distinguished from zero errors. Coalescing each term separately makes "zero" and "never emitted" the same visible flat line here, which is the honest reading for a counter that starts at zero.
panels.title: Internal RPC errors

panels.description:
Read the anonymous line; ignore the working set.

Garage's total RSS is not a health signal. H1 measured it moving 223 -> 1527 -> 365 MiB as object count rose monotonically, because ~98% of it is reclaimable page cache over the mmap'd LMDB metadata file, which the kernel drops under pressure. Anonymous memory -- the part that is actually unreclaimable and can OOM the container -- stayed flat at ~5 MiB throughout. A naive memory panel here would show 1.5 GB against a 2 GiB limit and look alarming while meaning nothing.

H1's pre-registered gate was anonymous RSS <= 512 MiB (measured: 5.7 MiB, against MinIO's 480.2 MiB). No threshold line is drawn, because the working-set series legitimately exceeds it and colouring the panel by it would recreate exactly the false alarm this panel exists to prevent.
panels.title: Memory -- anonymous vs reclaimable
